details:
**Reconquista**
The roughly 700-year process (c. 718–1492) by which Christian kingdoms of northern Iberia retook the peninsula from Muslim rule. It is the single most common topic in Spain questions, running from the founding of Asturias to the fall of Granada.

**Battle of Covadonga and Pelagius**
Around 718–722, the Visigothic noble Pelagius (Pelayo) defeated an Umayyad force at Covadonga, preserving the Christian Kingdom of Asturias. It is traditionally considered the start of the Reconquista and followed the 711 invasion led by Tariq ibn Ziyad that toppled the Visigothic Kingdom.

**Fall of Granada (1492) and Boabdil**
Granada, ruled by the Nasrid dynasty from the Alhambra palace, was the last Muslim state in Iberia. Its last emir, Boabdil (Muhammad XII), surrendered to Ferdinand and Isabella in 1492; legend says he wept at the mountain pass called "The Moor's Last Sigh" as he left, and he was briefly given lands in the Alpujarras before departing for Morocco.

**El Cid**
Rodrigo Díaz de Vivar, an 11th-century Castilian knight who fought for both Christian and Muslim rulers and conquered and ruled Valencia. He became Spain's national hero; legend says his horse was named Babieca ("stupid") and that his corpse was strapped onto his horse to rally the defenders of Valencia.

**Ferdinand and Isabella (the Catholic Monarchs)**
Ferdinand II of Aragon and Isabella I of Castile married in 1469, uniting the two crowns into what became modern Spain (their motto was "Tanto monta, monta tanto"). They completed the Reconquista, established the Spanish Inquisition under Tomás de Torquemada, and were the parents of Joanna the Mad and Catherine of Aragon, first wife of Henry VIII.

**Alhambra Decree**
The 1492 edict issued by Ferdinand and Isabella that expelled from Spain all Jews who refused to convert to Christianity. It was issued in the same year as the fall of Granada and Columbus's first voyage.

**Christopher Columbus and the Capitulations of Santa Fe**
Ferdinand and Isabella sponsored Columbus's 1492 voyage across the Atlantic, setting its terms in the Capitulations of Santa Fe. This launched the Spanish colonial empire in the Americas, including the viceroyalty of New Spain (Mexico).

**Taifa kingdoms, the Almoravids and the Almohads**
After the Caliphate of Córdoba collapsed in civil war in the early 11th century, al-Andalus split into small Muslim states called taifas. The North African Almoravid and later Almohad dynasties crossed into Iberia and took over the taifas; the Almohad caliph Muhammad al-Nasir was crushed by a Christian coalition at the Battle of Las Navas de Tolosa in 1212.

**Abd al-Rahman I and the Emirate of Córdoba**
An Umayyad prince who fled the Abbasid Revolution and founded the independent Emirate of Córdoba in 756, keeping the Umayyad dynasty alive in al-Andalus, the Arabic name for Muslim Iberia. Earlier, an Umayyad army that crossed from Iberia into Gaul was halted at the Battle of Tours (732).

**Charles V (Charles I of Spain)**
The Habsburg son of Joanna the Mad who ruled Spain and the Holy Roman Empire. He put down the Comuneros revolt, captured Francis I of France at the Battle of Pavia (1525), oversaw the Sack of Rome (1527), sponsored Magellan's circumnavigation, and called the Diet of Worms before abdicating in 1555–56 and retiring to a monastery.

**Philip II and the Spanish Armada**
Charles V's son, who married Mary I of England and later gained the Portuguese throne in the Iberian Union. He sent the Duke of Alba, who set up the "Council of Blood," to crush the Dutch Revolt led by William the Silent, and in 1588 launched an Armada against England that was defeated at Gravelines (Francis Drake had earlier raided Cádiz).

**Hispania and Saguntum**
The Roman name for the Iberian Peninsula. Hannibal's siege of Saguntum began the Second Punic War, Scipio Africanus won the region at the Battle of Ilipa, and Augustus later divided it into Baetica, Tarraconensis and Lusitania. The emperor Trajan was born there.

**Ferdinand VII, the Constitution of 1812 and the Carlist Wars**
Ferdinand VII was forced to abdicate during Napoleon's Peninsular War, while the Cortes of Cádiz wrote the liberal Constitution of 1812. A French army, the "Hundred Thousand Sons of Saint Louis," ended the Trienio Liberal in 1823. When his daughter Isabella II succeeded him in 1833, his brother Don Carlos's supporters launched the Carlist Wars.

**Spanish–American War and the USS Maine**
Spain was blamed for the 1898 explosion of the USS Maine in Havana Harbor, which helped spark war with the United States. In the resulting Treaty of Paris, Spain lost Cuba, Puerto Rico, Guam and the Philippines.

**Francisco Franco and the Spanish Civil War**
Franco's Nationalists defeated the Republicans in the Spanish Civil War (1936–39), and he ruled as dictator, backed by the Falange party, until his death in 1975. King Juan Carlos I then oversaw Spain's transition to democracy.
